metadata.title: TIMSS 2015: Highlights of Mathematics Achievement amongst Grade 5 South African Learners

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The TIMSS 2015 Numeracy assessment for Grade 5 in South Africa was administered in 2014 to 297 schools with 10,932 learners, using explicit and implicit stratified random sampling. Stratification variables included province, school type (public vs independent), and language of learning and teaching (Afrikaans, English, dual medium). The document describes the sampling design but does not report specific weight variable names (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the study is based on TIMSS/IEA sampling and reporting, it is treated as using complex survey weighting in the production of national estimates, even though the exact weight variables are not provided in the excerpt.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the TIMSS Numeracy 2015 Grade 5 South Africa sample collected in 2014. The study employed stratified random sampling with stratification by province, school type (public/independent), and language of learning and teaching (Afrikaans/English/dual medium). The excerpt does not specify additional analytic exclusions (e.g., minimum item completion, missing background questionnaire rules), so the analytic sample is treated as the full available TIMSS Numeracy Grade 5 sample for South Africa as described.

data.outcome_summary: This TIMSS 2015 Grade 5 highlights report describes mathematics achievement for South Africa using TIMSS Numeracy (TIMSS-N) results reported on the TIMSS mathematics scale. The overall average scale score is 376 (SE 3.4), far below the international centre point of 500, with 39% of learners above 400 and only 1.3% at the Advanced benchmark (>625). Achievement is strongly patterned by school type and context: independent schools show much higher shares at Intermediate/High/Advanced benchmarks, while public no-fee schools have the largest concentration below 400. Girls outperform boys by 16 points (statistically significant), and weekly bullying is associated with lower achievement (reported ~72-point gap vs almost never).
